chapter: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
title: Charley Reynolds takes over; hiring the show
summary: Wooding describes Ben Allen and Mike Green as Atlantic City's Black bosses, and how Charley Reynolds hired his band and the entertainers.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Now, when I come back from Detroit, a man, a fellow come to me and he said, "Sam, what are you doing?" And I said, "We just got back into town. We're not doing anything." Well, he said, "Charlie Reynolds is taking over old man Baron's, Ben Allen's, rather, old man Ben Allen's place." Now let me tell you about Ben Allen. Ben Allen was a -- there was two negroes in Atlantic City at that time that controlled the whole negro section. One was Ben Allen, and then, up North, up in the other part of the town, there was another fellow named Mike Green.

Now, these two fellows could HANDLE on any part of the sporting world and they could control anything that went on down there. But Ben Allen was getting old now, and he was tired of this business, so he turned the place over to Charley Reynolds. But Charley Reynolds was a younger fellow and he had his gambling going there and everything, so he wanted a good show. He figured that being at Kentucky and Arctic Avenue, that was the hub of the black belt. Where everybody, both the people who were good and the people who were bad, everybody circulated around there.

See, so, he said, 'Sam, you can bring a band in here.' I had about, let's see, I had five, six musicians at that time. He said, 'Come on in here and find me some girls that are good entertainers. And a man to go along with them.' So, that's when I picked up the two Ethels and another girl named Izzy Ringgold, which was a very good dancer and singer. In fact, she outsung most of the girls at that time. She was very good. And then I had a fellow called Snow Fisher.

Well, we worked all the summer. And, of course, being in the heart of town, there wasn't no laying off. You had to keep the music going all the time. Often, I'd keep the music going. So one night we started in at 9 o'clock. About 12 o'clock Ethel Waters got tired of jumping up every now and then, doing a song. So she said to Sam, 'Why don't you go an' urinate,
relieve yourself." She said, because, "And take a rest, because I'm tired of singing."
